processed_paragraphs.heading: SLOT 1: Introduction section
processed_paragraphs.content: This peer review addresses the Probabilistic Seismic Hazard Assessment conducted by WSP Canada Inc. for the Louvicourt Mine Tailings Storage Facility located in southwestern Quebec. The project pertains to a closed tailings storage facility owned by Teck Resources Ltd., with the analysis focused on Dam 1D at coordinates 48.135 degrees north latitude and 77.595 degrees west longitude. WSP undertook a site-specific seismic hazard assessment with the objective of quantifying earthquake ground motions for annual exceedance probabilities of 1/2,475, 1/5,000, and 1/10,000 years, corresponding approximately to return periods of 2,475, 5,000, and 10,000 years respectively. The SSSHA also included development of eight two-horizontal-component earthquake acceleration time histories amplitude-scaled to the 1/10,000 AEP mean uniform hazard spectrum. The purpose of this independent expert peer review performed by SRK is to evaluate the technical adequacy of the PSHA study, identify any gaps in methodology or data analysis, and assess compliance with current professional practice standards for seismic hazard assessment in stable continental regions. [@WSP2024]

processed_paragraphs.heading: SLOT 2: Tectonic regimes controlling seismicity
processed_paragraphs.content: The seismicity of the region within a radius of 1,000 km from the Louvicourt site is controlled by stable continental region tectonics characteristic of the Canadian Shield. The site is located within the North American Craton, which comprises ancient crystalline basement rocks and highly metamorphosed sedimentary units dating back more than 1 billion years. The Canadian Shield formed from the collision of Archean-age microcontinents during the Paleoproterozoic period (2.5 to 1.6 Ga), with subsequent volcanic activity creating volcanic arcs that accreted to existing Archean tectonic plates to form the ancient continent of Laurentia. The regional tectonic setting is intraplate, meaning that earthquake activity occurs within the interior of a stable continental plate rather than at active plate boundaries. This intraplate seismicity is generally characterized by lower earthquake occurrence rates compared to active tectonic margins, diffuse spatial distribution of epicenters, and absence of well-defined surface-rupturing active faults. The seismotectonic provinces in the region include the Superior Province (containing the Abitibi and Pontiac sub-provinces separated by the Cadillac-Larder Lake fault zone) and areas influenced by historical seismicity zones such as Charlevoix and the Ottawa-Gatineau region located several hundred kilometers to the east and southeast of the Louvicourt site. [@WSP2024]

processed_paragraphs.heading: SLOT 3: Source types in the model
processed_paragraphs.content: All seismic sources employed in the CanadaSHM6 model for the Louvicourt site are classified as Stable Continental Region sources. The PSHA uses the sixth-generation seismic hazard model of Canada developed by Natural Resources Canada, which divides Canada into three regional models: Southeastern Canada, Western Canada, and Eastern Arctic Canada. The Louvicourt TSF site falls within the Southeastern Canada model, which comprises three sub-models designated as Historical (H2), Regional (R2), and Hybrid (HY) with respective weights of 0.4, 0.2, and 0.4. Each sub-model consists of areal seismic sources (also termed background sources or area sources) that represent diffuse seismicity not associated with identified active faults. Within the 1,000 km region surrounding the site, no sources are classified as active crustal tectonic types associated with plate boundaries or subduction zones. The ground motion models applied in the assessment are specifically those developed for Central and Eastern North America, including the 17 NGA-East GMMs which are explicitly designed for stable continental regions. The major contributing seismic source zones identified through hazard decomposition are the Charlevoix source zone (CHV and CHVHY variants) and the Gatineau source zone, both representing intraplate seismic sources within the stable continental environment of southeastern Canada. [@WSP2024]

processed_paragraphs.heading: SLOT 5: Characteristic magnitudes and distances for rare events
processed_paragraphs.content: For rare events with annual exceedance probabilities in the range of 1/5,000 to 1/10,000 years, the PSHA disaggregation results provide characteristic magnitudes and distances that control the hazard. At the 1/5,000 AEP level, the modal magnitude bins range from $M_w$ 7.0-7.4 depending on spectral period, with modal distances predominantly in the 140-180 km range. Specifically, at PGA the modal magnitude is $M_w$ 7.2-7.4 with modal distance 140-160 km, at 0.2 second the modal magnitude is $M_w$ 7.2-7.4 with modal distance 140-160 km, at 0.5 second the modal magnitude is $M_w$ 7.0-7.2 with modal distance 160-180 km, and at 1.0 second the modal magnitude is $M_w$ 7.2-7.4 with modal distance 160-180 km. For the 1/10,000 AEP level, modal magnitudes remain in the $M_w$ 7.2-7.4 range across all spectral periods, with modal distances of 160-180 km. Mean magnitudes at 1/10,000 AEP range from $M_w$ 6.8-7.4 and mean distances range from 120 km to 240 km depending on spectral period. The dominant hazard contribution for these rare events comes from earthquakes with magnitudes approximately $M_w$ 6.8 to 7.5 occurring at source-to-site distances between 100 km and 200 km. Compared to the more frequent events, the rare events show a slight increase in characteristic magnitude and more consistent distance distributions across spectral periods, reflecting the contribution of the largest credible earthquakes from the Charlevoix and Gatineau seismic source zones. [@WSP2024]

processed_paragraphs.heading: SLOT 6: Active neotectonic faults identification
processed_paragraphs.content: The PSHA document indicates that no active neotectonic faults have been identified within 100 km of the Louvicourt site. Although major structural features exist in the region, including the Cadillac-Larder Lake fault zone located approximately 10 km from the site, these structures are not considered seismically active. The Cadillac-Larder Lake fault zone marks the boundary between the Abitibi and Pontiac sub-provinces of the Superior Province and represents a major structural complex formed during Archean tectonic events more than 2 billion years ago. Despite the proximity of this major fault zone to the site, several lines of evidence indicate it is not currently active: earthquake epicenters recorded in the region are widely distributed and generally not associated with mapped faults, there is no alignment of earthquake epicenters along the fault trace, the fault zone rocks are in a stable tectonic setting within the Canadian Shield, and there is no geomorphic evidence for past surface fault rupture during the Quaternary period. The seismic source model adopted from CanadaSHM6 does not include the Cadillac-Larder Lake fault zone or other regional faults as discrete seismic sources, instead treating all seismicity in the region as arising from diffuse areal sources. This approach is consistent with the characterization of the region as a stable continental interior where seismicity is not controlled by identifiable active fault structures. [@WSP2024]

processed_paragraphs.heading: SLOT 8: Executive summary of seismic record selection
processed_paragraphs.content: The seismic record selection process for the Louvicourt project involved development of two suites of eight two-horizontal-component earthquake acceleration time histories scaled to the 1/10,000 AEP mean uniform hazard spectrum. Two fundamental period values were provided for the Louvicourt TSF embankments: a shorter period $T_S$ in the range 0.25 to 0.37 seconds and a longer period $T_L$ of approximately 1.15 seconds, leading to development of separate suites for short-period and long-period ranges. The selection approach began with review of disaggregation results to identify representative causal parameters, selecting a modal scenario of $M_w$ 7.3 at 170 km rupture distance based on the 1/10,000 AEP hazard decomposition. Target secondary intensity measures including cumulative absolute velocity, Arias intensity, and significant durations were estimated and conditioned to the target spectrum at each fundamental period using an epsilon value of 1.5. Candidate ground motion records were compiled from the PEER NGA-West2 database for magnitudes $M_w$ 6.0 to 7.8 and distances 0 to 200 km, with relatively loose bounds justified by explicit consideration of secondary intensity measures. The NGA-East database was consulted but provided no records with magnitudes exceeding $M_w$ 5.85. Candidate motions were amplitude-scaled to achieve agreement with the target spectrum, with scaling generally kept within a range of 0.5 to 4.0 but with primary emphasis on spectral fit and secondary intensity measure compatibility rather than strict adherence to scaling limits. Final suite selection focused on achieving geometric mean horizontal response within 90 to 130 percent of the target spectrum across the period ranges of interest (0.062 to 0.62 seconds for short period, 0.23 to 2.3 seconds for long period) and reasonable agreement between empirical and conditional intensity measures. [@WSP2024]

processed_paragraphs.heading: SLOT 9: Adequacy of criteria for tectonic type
processed_paragraphs.content: The seismic record selection criteria employed show partial adequacy for the Stable Continental Region tectonic type of the Louvicourt area but exhibit important limitations. The selection approach correctly identifies the need for records compatible with SCR seismicity characteristics by referencing the NGA-East database, which contains ground motions from stable continental regions including central and eastern North America. However, the NGA-East database provided no suitable records with magnitudes exceeding $M_w$ 5.85, well below the target scenario magnitude of $M_w$ 7.3 and the modal disaggregation magnitudes of $M_w$ 7.0-7.4 that control the site hazard. Consequently, all selected records were sourced from the NGA-West2 database, which comprises ground motions recorded in active tectonic regions including California, Taiwan, Japan, and Italy with source mechanisms (strike-slip, reverse, reverse oblique, normal) and tectonic environments fundamentally different from the intraplate stable continental setting of southeastern Canada. To compensate for this tectonic incompatibility, the selection process employed secondary intensity measures (Arias intensity, cumulative absolute velocity, significant durations) conditioned to the site hazard and verified that scaled motions matched the target uniform hazard spectrum developed using NGA-East GMMs appropriate for stable continental regions. The assessment acknowledges that moderate-to-high-frequency ground motions attenuate faster in weaker active tectonic ground conditions compared to the stiffer bedrock conditions at the Louvicourt site ($V_{S30}$ = 1,853 m/s), necessitating selection of records with shorter source-to-site distances than the disaggregation results and application of some large scale factors to achieve spectral compatibility. While the selected motions have engineering intensity measures consistent with the stable continental hazard, the fundamental limitation remains that active tectonic recordings were used to represent stable continental earthquakes. [@WSP2024]

processed_paragraphs.heading: SLOT 10: Origin of 170 km rupture distance criterion
processed_paragraphs.content: The 170 km rupture distance criterion used for seismic record selection originates directly from the magnitude-distance disaggregation results for the 1/10,000 AEP hazard level. The disaggregation analysis presented in Figure 17 and Table 6 shows that the largest contribution to the 1/10,000 AEP seismic hazard at the Louvicourt site comes from earthquakes at source-to-site distances of approximately 100 to 200 km across both shorter spectral periods such as 0.2 seconds and longer spectral periods such as 1.0 second. The modal distance bin from the disaggregation is consistently 160-180 km for PGA and all spectral periods evaluated (0.2, 0.5, and 1.0 seconds) at the 1/10,000 AEP level. The 170 km value represents the center of this modal distance range and was selected along with the modal magnitude of $M_w$ 7.3 to define the causal parameters for estimating target secondary intensity measures and for creating the candidate ground motion catalogue. This distance criterion is specifically valid for the 1/10,000 AEP return period, which is the target hazard level for the earthquake acceleration time history development. The mean rupture distance from disaggregation varies from 120-140 km at PGA to 220-240 km at 1.0 second spectral period for the 1/10,000 AEP, but the 170 km value based on modal distance was selected as representative across the range of spectral periods relevant to both the short and long fundamental period analyses. For more frequent return periods (1/2,475 and 1/5,000 AEP), the disaggregation shows similar or somewhat larger distances, indicating that the 170 km criterion is not directly applicable to those lower hazard levels. [@WSP2024]

processed_paragraphs.heading: SLOT 12: Candidate catalog selection criteria
processed_paragraphs.content: The candidate ground motion catalog mentioned in point 3 of Chapter 8.0 was developed by the assessment team using the PEER NGA-West2 database with selection criteria defined by the project seismologists. Section 8.2 describes the candidate catalog development process, stating that the NGA-West2 database was used to create a catalogue of prospective ground motions ranging in magnitude from $M_w$ 6.0 to $M_w$ 7.8 and source-to-site distance from 0 to 200 km for each period range of interest, consistent with the disaggregation results showing controlling magnitudes of approximately $M_w$ 6.8 to 7.5 and distances of 100 to 200 km. The relatively loose bounds on earthquake magnitude and distance were intentionally employed because the ground motion selection process explicitly considered secondary intensity measures such as cumulative absolute velocity, Arias intensity, and significant durations. The technical rationale provided indicates that by explicitly considering secondary intensity measures, it becomes less important to target specific causal parameters such as earthquake magnitude, following the approach described by Baker (2021). Site parameters were not limited in creating the prospective ground motion catalogues to increase the number of prospective motions available for consideration. Scale factors applied to prospective ground motions were generally kept within the range of 0.5 to 4.0, though the scale factor was considered less important than comparison of secondary intensity measures and the fit of selected ground motions to the target spectrum. The NGA-East database was also consulted but was found to lack ground motion records with magnitudes greater than $M_w$ 5.85, eliminating it as a viable source for candidate motions matching the target scenario of $M_w$ 7.3. The selection from the candidate catalog was performed by WSP seismologists and involved amplitude scaling and evaluation against target spectral shape and secondary intensity measures to arrive at the final suites shown in Tables 10 and 11. [@WSP2024]

processed_paragraphs.heading: SLOT 13: Amplitude scaling factors
processed_paragraphs.content: The amplitude scaling factors applied to candidate ground motions and presented in Tables 10 and 11 span a wide range reflecting the challenges of matching active tectonic records to a stable continental region target spectrum. For the short period range suite (Table 10), the scale factors range from a minimum of 0.59 (RSN 5618, Iwate Japan earthquake) to a maximum of 8.28 (RSN 1833, Hector Mine earthquake). The eight records in the short period suite have scale factors of 1.11, 0.95, 8.28, 6.85, 3.19, 1.90, 0.59, and 0.80, with geometric mean approximately 2.3 and median approximately 1.5. For the long period range suite (Table 11), the scale factors range from a minimum of 0.64 (RSN 68, San Fernando earthquake) to a maximum of 2.87 (RSN 923, Big Bear earthquake). The eight records in the long period suite have scale factors of 0.64, 1.51, 2.67, 2.33, 2.87, 1.51, 1.71, and 0.77, with geometric mean approximately 1.6 and median approximately 1.6. Notably, two records in the short period suite (RSNs 1833 and 2927) have scale factors exceeding 6.0, which the report acknowledges were required to obtain a good match to the target spectrum in the shorter period range of interest. The assessment notes that these large scale factors were accepted because the selected motions have engineering intensity measures consistent with the hazard based on intraplate conditions and the focus was on achieving spectral compatibility and secondary intensity measure agreement rather than limiting scale factors. [@WSP2024]

processed_paragraphs.heading: SLOT 14: State of the art for amplitude scaling
processed_paragraphs.content: The literature and state of the art regarding amplitude scaling of real ground motion records indicates ongoing debate about appropriate limits and practices. Modern research published in 2023-2024 has evaluated the effects of amplitude scaling on structural response and found that when adequate attention is paid to selection criteria and secondary intensity measures, distribution of mean structural responses and intensity measures remain statistically unaffected by scaling level, with differences between demands obtained for different scaling levels being statistically insignificant at 90 percent confidence level. [@BullEarthqEng2023a] Contemporary guidance from earthquake engineering practice suggests that limits to scaling are appropriate when candidate time series are selected based only on magnitude, distance, and site condition, but records can be scaled by larger factors when selection criteria are based on properties of the scaled ground motion including spectral shape and secondary intensity measures rather than solely on scenario parameters. [@ArchCompMethods2023] Published research indicates that acceptable limits for amplitude scaling vary considerably across the professional community, ranging from no scaling allowed (factor of 1) to factors of 10 or more depending on the application and selection methodology. The engineering seismology literature emphasizes that scale factor limits should not be viewed as rigid constraints but rather should be evaluated in context of the overall ground motion selection approach, target spectrum characteristics, and whether secondary intensity measures are adequately represented. Recent studies have also demonstrated that amplitude scaling can introduce bias in structural drift estimates if not properly controlled, particularly when very large scale factors are applied without verification of intensity measure compatibility. [@EarthqEngStructDyn2022a] The consensus emerging from current research is that moderate scaling factors (approximately 0.5 to 4.0) are generally acceptable when combined with rigorous spectral matching and intensity measure verification, while very large scale factors exceeding 4.0 should be accompanied by careful justification and demonstration that the scaled motions preserve appropriate characteristics for the engineering application. [@ArchCompMethods2023]

processed_paragraphs.heading: SLOT 15: Reasonableness of large scaling factors
processed_paragraphs.content: The reasonableness of accepting amplification factors much greater than 2 or much less than 0.5 depends on the ground motion selection methodology and verification of engineering characteristics of the scaled records. Recent technical guidance documents indicate that individual scale factors should typically be limited to approximately 2.5 to minimize mean squared error for individual ground motions, though this limit may be exceeded when scaling the arithmetic mean spectrum of a suite to match a target spectrum, in which case scale factors should generally remain below 4.0 as recommended in modern practice standards. [@SoilDynEarthqEng2006] The ASCE 7 seismic design standards have evolved to permit scale factors up to approximately 4.0 for the mean spectrum of a ground motion suite when adequate spectral matching is achieved across the period range of interest. [@EarthqEngStructDyn2019] Research published in Earthquake Engineering & Structural Dynamics has investigated the effect of amplitude scaling limits on ground motion selection and concluded that excessively large scale factors (greater than 4.0) can distort the frequency content and intensity measure characteristics of real accelerograms, particularly when applied to individual records rather than to a suite mean. However, the literature also recognizes that rigid scale factor limits can make selection of suitable compatible actual accelerograms impossible for certain target spectra, especially when matching high-frequency ground motions for stiff site conditions using records from softer site conditions. The consensus from modern earthquake engineering research is that scale factors in the range 0.5 to 4.0 are generally acceptable for individual records when part of a suite whose geometric mean matches the target spectrum, while factors exceeding 4.0 or below 0.5 require specific justification demonstrating that engineering intensity measures of the scaled records remain representative of the target hazard scenario. Studies emphasize that verification of secondary intensity measures such as cumulative absolute velocity, Arias intensity, and significant duration provides essential validation that scaled records maintain appropriate characteristics even when scale factors are outside conventional limits. [@EarthqEngStructDyn2022a]

processed_paragraphs.heading: SLOT 16: Table 10 and 11 selection criteria verification
processed_paragraphs.content: The seismic records presented in Tables 10 and 11 show partial compliance with the criteria established at the beginning of Chapter 8.0 but also exhibit significant deviations from stated selection principles. The established criteria specified magnitude $M_w$ 7.3 and rupture distance 170 km as representative causal parameters based on disaggregation, with relatively loose bounds (magnitude $M_w$ 6.0 to 7.8, distance 0 to 200 km) justified by explicit consideration of secondary intensity measures. Examination of Table 10 for the short period suite shows selected record magnitudes ranging from $M_w$ 6.0 to 7.13, with five of eight records having magnitudes below $M_w$ 6.9, substantially lower than the target $M_w$ 7.3 scenario. Rupture distances in Table 10 range from 11 km to 73 km, all significantly shorter than the 170 km criterion and well below the lower bound of the 160-180 km modal disaggregation bin. Table 11 for the long period suite shows somewhat better magnitude agreement with magnitudes ranging from $M_w$ 6.46 to 7.62, including two records at or above $M_w$ 7.0, but rupture distances range from 23 km to 159 km with six of eight records having distances less than 65 km, again substantially shorter than the 170 km criterion. The criteria for period range of interest were met, with short period suite scaled for 0.062 to 0.62 seconds and long period suite scaled for 0.23 to 2.3 seconds as specified. Site ground conditions ($V_{S30}$) were not limited in the criteria and show substantial variation in the tables (312 to 826 m/s) compared to the target site condition of 1,853 m/s. Scale factors vary from 0.59 to 8.28 with two values exceeding the stated general range of 0.5 to 4.0. The assessment justifies these deviations by noting that the primary focus was on achieving geometric mean spectral compatibility and matching conditional secondary intensity measures rather than strict adherence to magnitude-distance criteria, and that shorter distances were necessary to capture high-frequency content for the stiff site condition when using records from softer active tectonic sites. [@WSP2024]

processed_paragraphs.heading: SLOT 17: SCR records confirmation from tables
processed_paragraphs.content: None of the records shown in Tables 10 and 11 are from Stable Continental Regions. Table 10 for the short period range includes records from: North Palm Springs California (reverse oblique mechanism, active San Andreas fault system), Hector Mine California (strike-slip mechanism, Mojave Desert active faulting), Chi-Chi Taiwan earthquakes (strike-slip and reverse mechanisms, active collision zone between Philippine Sea Plate and Eurasian Plate), Umbria Marche Italy (normal faulting, active Apennine extensional tectonics), and Iwate Japan (reverse mechanism, active subduction zone). Table 11 for the long period range includes records from: San Fernando California (reverse mechanism, active Transverse Ranges), Loma Prieta California (reverse oblique mechanism, active San Andreas system), Landers California (strike-slip, Eastern California Shear Zone), Big Bear California (strike-slip, Southern California active faulting), and additional Chi-Chi Taiwan records (reverse and reverse oblique mechanisms, active plate boundary). All these earthquake events occurred in active tectonic environments characterized by plate boundary processes, high strain rates, and well-defined active fault systems, representing fundamentally different seismotectonic settings from the stable continental region classification of southeastern Canada. The assessment acknowledges this limitation in Section 8.2, noting that the NGA-East database which contains stable continental region records lacked ground motions with magnitudes greater than $M_w$ 5.85, making it impossible to select SCR records matching the target scenario magnitude of $M_w$ 7.3 and controlling hazard magnitudes of $M_w$ 6.8 to 7.5. The selection of active tectonic records was therefore a consequence of the unavailability of suitable large-magnitude recordings from stable continental regions rather than a preferred approach. The assessment justifies this choice by demonstrating that the selected and scaled motions achieve compatibility with the target uniform hazard spectrum developed using stable continental region ground motion models (NGA-East GMMs) and that secondary intensity measures of the scaled records are consistent with the conditional intensity measures estimated for stable continental earthquakes. [@WSP2024]
